questions.question: Three overlapping circles inside a rectangle divide the sample space into:
options: Six regions
Three regions
Eight regions
Twelve regions

questions.question: If a question says '12 do choir AND drama' (no 'only'), the exactly-two region gets:
options: 12 minus the centre count, because the and-count includes those doing all three
12, straight in
12 plus the centre count
Double the centre count

questions.question: In the survey of 120 learners, the number doing NO activity is:
P(a random learner does at least two activities) equals:
Drawing without replacement means the second-stage branches must:
options: Copy the first-stage probabilities exactly
Always be equal to a half
Keep the original denominator of 6
Be conditioned on the branch you sit on — the remaining sweets have changed

questions.question: With 4 orange and 2 mint sweets drawn without replacement, P(orange then orange) is:
P(one sweet of each flavour) is found by:
options: Adding the two qualifying paths: 8/30 + 8/30 = 8/15
Multiplying the two qualifying paths together
Taking 1 minus P(orange then orange)
Averaging P(orange) and P(mint)

questions.question: The audit for any completed tree diagram is:
options: Every branch must equal a half
All path products must sum to exactly 1
The number of paths must equal the number of sweets
The longest path must be the most likely

questions.question: In the 160-learner table, P(a random learner is a boy who cycles) is:
Marginal probabilities such as P(cycles) are read from:
options: The row and column totals in the margins
The centre cell of the table
The smallest cell in the column
The grand total divided by four

questions.question: Gender and transport are independent in the original table because:
options: Boys and girls have equal totals
More learners walk than cycle
The table has two rows and two columns
P(boy) × P(cycles) = 0,375 × 0,4 = 0,15, exactly matching the cell probability

questions.question: Another sign of that independence inside the numbers is:
options: The grand total is exactly 160
The cycling rate is 40% among boys AND 40% among girls — the rows tell one story
The margins are all even numbers
Walkers outnumber cyclists in both rows

subtopics.title: Choosing the Tool and Mixing the Rules

questions.question: Sequence language — 'first', 'then', 'without replacement' — calls for:
options: A contingency table
A three-circle Venn diagram
A tree diagram
The complement rule only

questions.question: A population classified by two characteristics — like gender and transport — calls for:
options: A contingency table with margins
A tree diagram with four branches
A single circle
An ogive

questions.question: Wind has probability 0,4; the team wins with 0,35 if windy and 0,7 if calm. P(win) is:
That weather calculation uses the tree rules:
options: Multiply along each path, then add the paths where the team wins
Add along each path, then multiply the paths
Multiply all four given numbers
Subtract the smaller path from the larger

subtopics.title: Eight Rooms, Filled from the Middle

questions.question: In the house picture, the middle room is filled first because:
options: It is the biggest room in the house
Its number is the only one that always arrives clean, needing no interpretation
The stoep outside depends on it directly
The heroes arrive earliest

questions.question: The word that decides whether to subtract the middle room from a shared-room count is:
options: 'And' on its own
'Neither'
'At least'
'Only' or 'but not'

questions.question: The 25 learners on the stoep represent:
options: Those who do no activity at all
Those who do all three activities
The chess-only members
Those who do exactly one activity

questions.question: 'Exactly one activity' is answered by pointing at:
options: The middle room only
The three loyal single-activity rooms: 63 of 120
Every room including the stoep
The three shared rooms

questions.question: 'The packet remembers' means:
options: The sweets are drawn in flavour order
Orange sweets are stickier than mint
The first draw has no effect on the second
Each draw changes the world the next draw faces — the events are dependent

questions.question: Following one path of the tree — orange THEN orange — is:
options: An and-story, so the probabilities multiply
An or-story, so the probabilities add
A complement, so subtract from 1
Independent, so the branches are equal

questions.question: After a mint sweet is eaten first, the second draw's branches are:
options: 3/5 orange and 2/5 mint
4/5 orange and 1/5 mint
2/3 orange and 1/3 mint
1/5 orange and 4/5 mint

questions.question: The 'receipt' at the end of every tree question is:
options: Counting that the tree has exactly four branches
Checking the first-stage probabilities are equal
Adding all path products and confirming they total exactly 1
Multiplying all path products together

subtopics.title: The Register at the School Gate

questions.question: In the register picture, independence between gender and transport means:
options: The rows tell the same story — cycling rates match across genders
Boys and girls are equal in number
Every cell of the table is equal
Nobody cycles to school

questions.question: In the original register, the cycling rate among boys is 24 out of 60, which is:
In the tilted data — 30 of 60 boys cycling against 34 of 100 girls — the verdict becomes:
options: Independent, because the cycle total is still 64
Dependent: the rows split apart, 50% against 34%, and the product test fails
Mutually exclusive
Impossible to judge from a table

questions.question: A complete answer to a table independence question ends with:
options: The grand total, circled
A redrawn version of the table
A written sentence giving the verdict with both compared numbers in it
The percentages only, no conclusion
